# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Language models routinely act on information they have not written down. A model
completing a rhyming couplet selects its rhyme before it writes the line that ends
in it [@lindsey2025biology; @hanna2026latent]. A model asked for the result of a
calculation, or to make a choice and reveal it later, must hold or reconstruct that
content across the tokens it writes in between. How such unwritten information
reaches the position that uses it is a basic question about autoregressive
computation. It is also a practical one. Chain-of-thought monitoring assumes that
the reasoning relevant to a decision passes through, or can be recovered from, the
text the model writes [@korbak2025monitorability; @baker2025monitoring]. The
central risk to that assumption is decision-relevant content that the model uses
but never states in its text [@pfau2024dots; @roger2023steganography;
@turpin2023unfaithful; @chen2025reasoning].

In a transformer, information present at one position can reach a later position
by three paths (@fig-overview A). It can be **emitted**: it changes the tokens the
model writes, and those tokens are read back as input. It can be **retrieved**: the
later position attends directly to the position where the information originates,
or to the visible text from which it can be recomputed. Or it can be **relayed**,
that is, carried forward: intermediate positions, including the tokens the model
generates, read it and pass it on to later ones. The three paths differ in what a
monitor can see. Emitted information is in the text. Retrieved information stays at
a fixed position of the context, where it can be read or probed. Relayed information
travels through the model's own output without appearing in it. Relay is therefore
the path by which a model could hold or update content across a chain of thought
that never states it. Between retrieval and relay sits a fourth possibility that
turns out to matter: a **stored copy**, written once into a structural position of
the prompt next to the source and read directly from there.

Prior work establishes that planning signals exist and are causally used: they are
decodable ahead of time [@pal2023futurelens; @wu2024plan; @men2024lookahead],
visible in attribution graphs [@lindsey2025biology; @hanna2026latent], and steerable
at the planning site [@maar2026plan; @ma2026plan; @jacopin2026improvisation]. These
methods locate where a plan is formed or can be changed. They do not measure which
path the plan takes to the position where it is used.

We introduce **route accounting**, a decomposition of an intervention's effect by
path (@sec-method). A donor's hidden states are written at the source positions, and
the effect is measured where the information is used. Clamping the states of chosen
groups of positions to their clean or edited values, at every layer, isolates each
path. Emission is separated from persistence by fixing the generated text. Within
persistence, direct retrieval is separated from relay, and relay is split by position
into the stored copy, the late lookup just before the target, and early relay along
the generated text. For every group of positions we measure what the group achieves
alone (interventional sufficiency) and what is lost without it (interventional
necessity), and we report the interaction between paths explicitly. Because a method
that never finds relay would be uninformative, we validate route accounting on
induction [@olsson2022induction], where relay through the copied token's position is
the known mechanism. Relay is the largest path in all nine models tested. The committed criterion (relay above 80%, direct retrieval near zero) holds cleanly in four and partly in five, for reasons we identify (@sec-control).

Applied to four tasks in 15 checkpoints from three model families, route accounting
finds a consistent principle, within the settings tested (short generated spans,
thinking disabled): **look it up, don't carry it**. Models retrieve unwritten
information rather than relay it. They read it near the point of use from a fixed
position of the prompt: the position where it originates, or a copy stored at a
structural token next to it (@tbl-map).

- *Visible plans.* Rhyme plans reach the rhyme mainly by direct retrieval of the rhyme
  word: 68 to 95% of persistence in every configuration but one (@sec-lookup). Early
  relay along the generated line is at most 1% of persistence: by sufficiency in all
  21 runs, and by necessity in the 17 where it was measured.
- *Computed values.* Donor states at every position after the source move the answer by
  at most 2.4% of the source effect in variable chains, and 6% in sums, while edits of
  the source remain effective. This near-zero downstream patch effect is consistent
  with the answer re-reading its visible sources.
- *Written values.* When the model writes its intermediate values, the answer follows
  them: emission accounts for 83 to 100% of the effect (@sec-emission).

A regularity found under favourable conditions is only as strong as the tests that
could have broken it. We therefore test the principle in three settings chosen to make
carrying useful or to make it invisible, each with a decision rule committed before the
result (@sec-stress). They bound the principle rather than confirm it.

- **Recurrent memory.** In the Qwen3.5 hybrid, three of every four layers can pass
  information forward only through a recurrent state, so relay is available to most  of the network [@yang2025gateddeltanet]. The test asks which route the model uses
  when both exist. When the donor signal may enter only through the recurrent layers at
  the source, it produces 2 to 4% of persistence at 4B, 9B and 27B parameters, below the
  committed stop line; entering through the attention layers, it produces 95 to 97%.
- **Distance.** Beyond Gemma 3's 1,024-token local window, five of six layers cannot
  read the source [@gemma3]. As filler grows from 0 to 2,000 tokens, the 27B model
  shifts from reading the rhyme word toward the stored copy at the line's final token,
  which becomes necessary for about half of persistence. The shift is gradual, steepest
  as line 1 leaves the window. Relay through the generated text (the cue and line 2,
  including its last three positions) is 9 to 13% of persistence by sufficiency at every nonzero
  distance. This block has not been split into early relay and late lookup, and it
  falls between the committed stop (10%) and go (25%) lines, so it is a boundary case
  whose early-relay contribution remains unresolved. In the 12B model, which stores little at the line end, the plan fades
  with distance, already inside the window, and relay never takes over.
- **Hidden content.** A choice that a reader cannot infer from the text is the case
  monitoring cares about most. Information specific to a secret pick is stored after
  the list, at a few predictable, low-content tokens: the punctuation that closes the
  list or the instruction, and a function word or possessive token of the instruction, which at 4B, 12B and 27B moves when the instruction is reworded. The reveal reads it there. The intervening sentence never
  names the pick and has no measurable causal effect on it through emission. Relay
  through that sentence is at most 2% of the text-swap effect, although in Qwen3-32B and the Qwen3.5 hybrids it is one eighth to one fifth of the
  small stored part.

The one route that grows is the stored copy, and it grows in three ways (@sec-storage).
It grows with scale. The copy at the line's final token (the comma in chat prompts,
the newline in plain prompts) appears at 14B and above in Qwen3 and at 12B to 27B in
Gemma 3. It is also present in the base checkpoints we tested, so it most likely arises in
pretraining. It grows
with distance: beyond the attention window it is necessary for about half of the
plan's effect. And it is where hidden, pick-specific information is kept, at
segment-closing punctuation and function words or possessive tokens of the prompt. Stored copies thus sit
at a few predictable tokens next to their sources, which makes them a natural target
for monitoring internal state. The same analysis reconciles published accounts of
where the rhyme plan lives. The plan is read from the rhyme word [@hanna2026latent],
and it is also placed at the line boundary [@lindsey2025biology; @ma2026plan]. These
are two lookup sites that coexist, in proportions that depend on scale, family and
prompt format.

**Contributions.**

1. Route accounting: a path-level decomposition of intervention effects in
   autoregressive generation. It separates emission from persistence, direct
   retrieval from relay, and the stored copy, the late lookup and early relay from one
   another. It reports interventional sufficiency, necessity and interaction for every
   group of positions, and is validated on a positive control.
2. A principle with its evidence and its scope: in the settings tested, unwritten
   information is looked up, not carried. The evidence covers visible plans, computed
   values and hidden choices, across families, sizes, prompt formats and instruct
   versus base checkpoints. It holds under the published feature steering of
   @hanna2026latent as well as under state edits.
3. Three stress tests with decision rules committed before their results (recurrent
   memory, attention distance, hidden content). They bound where the principle holds
   and quantify the largest deviation we observe.
4. The emergence of a stored copy at the line's final token at 14B and above, and a
   reconciliation of the published accounts of rhyme planning.

Where unwritten information travels. Each cell gives the share of the effect that
travels by a path, as a range over the models tested; the denominator is persistence
unless stated. *Looked up*: the target reads the source, a copy stored at a structural
token next to it, or positions just before the target that read it (late lookup).
*Carried*: the effect passes through intermediate positions (for tasks, early relay
along the generated text). Observability: *visible* content can be recovered by a
reader of the text; *hidden* content cannot. Dashes mark cells that the design rules
out. Sections and figures give the full results with 95% intervals.

:::
